Trump admin pick to oversee a conspiracy investigation into president’s foes resigns after DOJ clashes
description: The Trump administration’s pick to oversee a conspiracy investigation into the president’s foes has resigned under pressure from the Justice Department.
fullText:
The Trump administration's pick to oversee a conspiracy investigation into the president's foes has resigned under pressure from the Justice Department.

Joe diGenova stepped down from his role overseeing DOJ's vast so-called conspiracy investigation amid disagreements with top Justice Department officials over the pace of the south Florida-based probe that was intended to pursue possible charges against a swath of Donald Trump's top political foes, according to people briefed on the matter.

DiGenova's resignation came after a series of clashes with top Justice officials, including one in recent days with someone who advised him he had lost the confidence of his superiors, one of the people briefed on the discussions said.

"It was an honor and privilege to serve the president and the department," diGenova told CNN in a brief telephone interview, adding in a later statement, "As an old prosecutor of more than 50 years, I make cases the old fashioned way: witnesses, evidence, etc. That takes time." He declined to discuss the internal disputes that led to his resignation.

His departure is the latest upheaval for an investigation that diGenova took over in April, vowing that he could bring charges in 30 days, after the ouster of Maria Medetis Long, a seasoned career prosecutor who previously oversaw it. Medetis Long had balked at bringing charges more quickly.

The conspiracy probe is examining what Justice Department officials believe are possible crimes associated with government investigations into Trump stretching as far back as the 2016 Russian election interference inquiry and culminating with the federal charges against Trump in the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot and Mar-a-Lago classified documents cases.

Former CIA Director John Brennan, former FBI Director James Comey and others have been among the former government officials whose conduct is being scrutinized in the investigation, CNN has previously reported.

DiGenova is a longtime Washington lawyer and former Washington, DC, US attorney who briefly represented the president in one of the earlier Justice Department probes that is part of the conspiracy investigation.

After taking over the conspiracy probe in April, being named counselor to the attorney general, diGenova has overseen an uptick of witness interviews and in recent days grand jury testimony from witnesses in the case, according to people briefed no the matter. But despite expectations at Justice Department headquarters that charges could be brought as soon as this month, the case appears to still be a work in progress.

In the wake of diGenova's resignation, a portrait is emerging of an investigation unmoored from a lack of leadership with more than a dozen prosecutors assigned to chasing disparate targets and little to show for their efforts, according to two people familiar with the investigation.

"Joe came in pretty hot," one of the people familiar with the probe told CNN. "He had a lot of things he wanted to look into."

After initial signs that prosecutors would start with a relatively straightforward case, seeking charges against Brennan for alleged false statements in congressional testimony, diGenova decided he wanted to pursue more targets in a broader case, according one of the people familiar with the investigation. The source described it as "going down 900 rabbit holes."

"He was missing the forest for the trees," the source briefed on the probe told CNN.

What's more, the lack of focus caused acrimony inside the team led by diGenova, who was operating mostly from an office in Fort Pierce, Florida. Career lawyers assigned to the case were met with angry tirades from diGenova and were at times sidelined, according to one of the people familiar with the investigation.

At Justice Department headquarters, dissatisfaction grew to include the performance of US Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who since last year has repeatedly promised to bring charges in the investigation, the two sources familiar with the probe said.

Justice Department officials always intended Quiñones, as the top Senate-confirmed prosecutor in the district, to continue to oversee the probe, the people familiar said. The appointment of diGenova was a clear sign that Justice Department leadership didn't have confidence that Quiñones could deliver, one of them added.

In a recent clash with top Justice officials, Quiñones sought to disavow any responsibility for what has gone wrong with the investigation, one person familiar with the investigation told CNN. Quiñones was told to stop traveling to Washington and elsewhere and to focus on his job in Miami, a person familiar with the investigation said.

A spokesperson for Quiñones didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

With the latest ouster, the investigation is expected to continue and a possible standalone case could come more quickly, people familiar with the investigation said.

Top Justice officials made clear that "moving faster on cases," was the priority for all prosecutors, a person familiar with the investigation said.

The pressure to bring a case comes from the top. Trump himself has expressed his frustrations about the slow pace of bringing charges against foes he believes unfairly targeted him in the past. He has expressed his discontent in social media posts and in meetings with department leaders.

At a White House gathering with a group of US attorneys, Trump complained that some were weak and that they needed to move more quickly to deliver on his agenda, CNN previously reported. He fired former Attorney General Pam Bondi in part because of these complaints.

DiGenova laid out some of his vision for the Fort Pierce, Florida-based conspiracy investigation in an April 2 appearance on Rudy Giuliani's podcast in which he decried delays in bringing indictments in the probe. He accused Bondi of blocking plans to appoint him to run the civil rights section in the Miami US Attorney's office where the conspiracy probe is being run.

"If she had not done that, we would have indictments brought in the last two months," diGenova said at the time.

Victoria Toensing, diGenova's wife, who later joined him on his south-Florida prosecution team, appeared alongside him on the podcast.

She said it was a mistake to indict Comey, the former FBI director, in Virginia last year, a case that was later dismissed.

"I never as attorney general would have allowed the one count against Comey in Virginia, I would have saved it for the vast conspiracy in Fort Pierce," she said.

DiGenova agreed, adding "You do the same thing with [New York Attorney General] Letitia James. You don't charge her in Virginia on mortgage fraud. You include her on a massive conspiracy count down in Miami, with a bunch of people beginning in 2017."

He also named former President Barack Obama and others in his administration as possible targets.

"Put Obama in the grand jury and let's have a fight over his testimony," he said.

It's not clear how far diGenova managed to get in his pursuit of Obama and other possible targets of his investigation. Toensing also is expected to depart the office.

This story has been updated with additional details.

CNN's Kaitlan Collins contributed to this report.

title: As Trump dominates convention, some Republicans quietly ask who comes next
description: JD Vance delivered the keynote speech to end the party's convention - but the president still took centre stage, the BBC's Daniel Bush writes.
fullText:
Watch: Has Trump won over voters with his midterm convention?

Republicans descended on Dallas this week to turn their midterm prospects around, hoping an unprecedented convention dominated by President Donald Trump would energise voters ahead of the November election.

Many left the gathering - billed ahead of time by supporters as a "Trump-a-palooza" political fest - just as worried about the party's chances in 2026, and wondering what the Republicans' future will look like after the president leaves office.

Vice-President JD Vance, who is widely viewed as a top contender to succeed Trump, offered his a party a glimpse of its potential future during his keynote address on Thursday night.

"We've got to take care of business this November," Vance told the crowds.

"Then we'll worry about what comes next."

His speech was interrupted at one point by chants of "48" - a nod to Trump's successor, who will become the 48th US president if they win in 2028. Vance let the chant linger briefly before waving it away.

Over the two-day event, party activists were split on the wisdom of holding a midterm convention featuring a president who has record low approval ratings, and amid public frustration over the economy and war with Iran.

"I think it will make a difference. If anything it allows us to test the [campaign] message in front of a large audience," Jeff Ryer, the Virginia Republican Party chairman, told the BBC.

Others said the president's rambling, nearly two-hour convention speech on Wednesday wouldn't sway voters weighing whether to keep Republicans in power in Congress.

Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance to retake control of the House and the Senate is also in play, though viewed as more of a long shot for the party.

"Do I wish Trump gave a shorter speech? Sure, but that's not who he is," said one Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer a blunt view of Trump's convention appearance.

The source added that Trump's plea for voters to pretend as if he's on the ballot would fall flat.

"I don't think saying 'pretend I'm on the ballot' will work. He's not," the person said.

Is Trump's $5,000 pledge a sign of panic?

The convention offered a stark reminder that the Trump era is heading toward its final chapter.

Trump's presence loomed over the proceedings at the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas.

Republican House and Senate candidates lavished the president with praise in speeches, and supporters showed up wearing the red Maga hats that have become synonymous with Trump's political movement.

The gathering was just two days, but still had the look and feel of the traditional four-day conventions staged by both parties in presidential election years. Organisers distributed signs and unleashed a balloon drop at the end as live music blared.

Republicans had never held a midterm convention before.

Vikki Consiglio, a party activist from Georgia, said it showcased Trump's ability to shake up political norms and capture the nation's attention.

Evidence of that came when Trump pledged in his speech to make a payment of $5,000 to all American adults if Republicans retained control of Congress.

"He's a visionary. This whole convention is nothing but a vision," Consiglio said.

But even as convention goers cheered Trump on, many seemed eager to discuss the 2028 presidential election.

"I'm very concerned about the next 10, 15, 20 years. I'm absolutely thinking about the future of the party," said Aiden Buzzetti, the president of The Bull Moose Project, a pro-Trump group.

Buzzetti, who is 26, credited Trump with reshaping Republican politics, but said at the same time he was looking forward to a "new generation of conservative leaders."

In interviews with the BBC, attendees at the convention most often mentioned Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as the top contenders to replace Trump.

"Trump needs to pass the torch. We need to look forward," said Sandy Money, a Republican from Arizona who attended the convention. "I love Vance. But Rubio is my choice" if he runs in 2028, she said.

Trump has openly mused about Rubio and Vance's chances to succeed him.

But Vance and Rubio have deflected speculation about their political futures.

Rubio was on a diplomatic trip to Ecuador during the convention, so he wasn't among the small handful of cabinet officials who attended the festivities in Dallas.

The Trump administration has delivered "a great record of achievement," Vance argued, including improving the economy, strengthening border security and lowering the cost of prescription drugs.

Vance said the contrast was clear with a Democratic Party that he argued had shifted radically to the left and turned into the "party of crazy".

The vice-president also made a direct appeal to undecided voters, saying he wanted to win over "the people who are still making up their minds".

Never one to cede the spotlight, Trump returned to the stage on Thursday night after Vance to round off the convention.

For the president, the question of his successor was overshadowed by more immediate concerns.

"You know what happens if you don't vote?" he asked the gathered crowd. "You go to hell."

title: US judge blocks Trump administration's 'loyalty' question for job applicants
description: A federal judge on Friday blocked U.S.
fullText:
BOSTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - A federal judge on Friday blocked U.S. President Donald Trump's administration from continuing to ask applicants for civil service jobs throughout the government to respond to ‌what unions described as a partisan "loyalty question."

U.S. District Judge George O'Toole in Boston sided with three ‌unions representing government workers who sued last year after the administration began asking applicants for nonpartisan federal jobs to write essays explaining how ​they would help advance Trump's policies and executive orders.

The unions, including the American Federation of Government Employees, argued the question mandated by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) unlawfully politicized the hiring process for career government workers by attempting to assess their support for the Republican president.

O'Toole, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the question had been asked of ‌applicants to positions ranging from an ⁠air traffic control specialist to a crane operator to a nuclear materials courier.

He said the unions' members reasonably interpreted it as an attempt to determine the applicants' political views, even ⁠though the Civil Service Reform Act bars making employment decisions for such jobs on the basis of political affiliation.

"The plaintiffs are thus likely to succeed in showing that there is no legitimate governmental interest in inquiring into the political beliefs of ​applicants ​to federal civil service vacancies," O'Toole wrote.

The judge halted the ​use of the question on grounds that it ‌likely violated the Administrative Procedure Act by infringing on speech rights under the U.S. Constitution's First Amendment.

Lawyers for the unions at the liberal group Democracy Forward welcomed the ruling, saying that over 70,000 federal job postings had included the question, undermining what is supposed to be a merit-based hiring system.

"Requiring federal job applicants to answer politically motivated questions goes against the very nature of the nonpartisan civil service," AFGE National President Everett Kelley said in a ‌statement.

title: Murphy beats Trump in deciding frame to reach semis

fullText:
Shaun Murphy snatched a thrilling final-frame victory over Judd Trump to reach the semi-finals of the English Open.

World number seven Murphy moved 5-4 ahead before Trump, the world number three, cleared 112 to take the match to a decider.

Murphy managed to overcome his English compatriot in a nervy final frame, helped by some deft safety play, to set up a semi-final against Mark Williams.

Williams withstood a fightback from fellow Welshman Liam Davies to book his spot in the semi-finals with a 6-3 victory.

Williams was level at 2-2 at the interval but pulled clear and eventually sealed his victory with a 112 clearance.

England's Kyren Wilson was left scoreless in the first three frames as Ding Junhui cruised to a 6-2 victory.

Wilson briefly threatened a comeback, winning the next two frames to reduce the deficit to 3-2, but China's Ding quickly regained control and took the final three frames to seal his place in the final four.

Ding will face Ali Carter in the semi-finals, who produced an excellent late display to edge past Zhou Yuelong 6-5 by winning three frames in a row.

Zhou had been leading 5-3, but Carter was able to turn it around from frame nine onwards, making the most of Zhou missing a routine yellow, then winning the next 80-39 before dominating in the decider.

Can The 'Best Showman In Politics' Deliver Again? Gop Bets On Trump At Historic Midterm Convention

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) are preparing to propose a rule that would eliminate an existing grace period for visa holders who can't find a job, according to an unpublished document posted to the Federal Register.

Under current immigration laws, holders of certain visas, particularly H-1B visas, which are non-immigration visas that allow employers to sponsor skilled workers with Bachelor's degrees or higher, get a 60-day grace period to find a new job if they lose the employment tied to their visa.

The new rule proposal would eliminate that grace period, according to the document.

"This proposal restores a direct relationship between an alien's nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden," the document reads.

A noncitizen would have to immediately leave the U.S. if no longer working for an employer linked to a visa status if the rule were to be implemented.

Us State Department Has Yanked More Than 175K Visas Under Trump Administration So Far

"DHS believes that restoring the expectation that aliens depart the United States upon cessation of the employment or activity upon which the alien's status was based, would better promote program integrity and be more consistent with statutory purpose," the rule proposal reads.

The agency also claimed that eliminating the grace period would greatly reduce administrative burden "as the process of determining when the up to 60-day grace period may apply, reviewing the information submitted, and determining whether to shorten or eliminate the grace period may be time consuming and complex for the agency and confusing or unpredictable for the petitioner, alien and the alien's dependents."

America's Broken Legal Immigration System Is Replacing Us Workers By Design

Before 2017, the document states, there was no 60-day grace period. But in 2016, DHS established the grace period in a rule that came into effec Jan. 17, 2017, three days before President Donald Trump first took office.

DHS also wrote that the rule's elimination would favor U.S. workers because employers who previously filled jobs with foreign workers would have less foreign-born labor to choose from.

"DHS assumes that almost all these entities would offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers, go through the I-129 petition process to sponsor nonimmigrant workers, or reassign the work to other current employees. DHS acknowledges that some of these petitioners may incur a temporary loss of productivity due to labor turnover," the rule proposal reads.

The unpublished rule is scheduled to publish Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, according to the Federal Register. It will then be subject to a two-month period of public comment before becoming law.

fullText:
Saudi Arabia is urging Washington to take direct military action against Iran-backed Houthis, Fox News Digital learned after the terrorist group seized key positions along Yemen's Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday.

The dramatic strengthening of Houthi's positioning along the coastline of Yemen is in one of the world's most important shipping choke points — a narrow passage that links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, which has been used as a bypass as the Iran war continues to severely disrupt shipping, especially of oil, through the Strait of Hormuz.

The rapid advance on Friday triggered urgent discussions at the highest levels in Riyadh and Washington, and a source familiar with the matter tells Fox News Digital that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis.

New Risk For U.s. Consumers As Iran-backed Attacks Threaten A Second Major Oil Chokepoint

The Houthis reached the strategic island of Mayyun, also known as Perim, after Yemeni government forces withdrew and also took the mainland coastal town of Dhubab, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Friday.

Fox News Digital independently confirmed key elements of an Axios report with a source familiar with the matter, who said the crown prince spoke with Trump a few times over the past 24 hours about the escalating situation in Yemen.

The U.S. does not want to take direct military action for now, but Trump told bin Salman that Washington would assist Saudi Arabia with intelligence and targeting support, according to the source.

The source also confirmed that U.S. Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper traveled to Saudi Arabia for coordination talks.

The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the calls or whether additional U.S. military action is under consideration.

Iran's Biggest Weapon Against The U.s. May Be Slipping Away, Experts Say

The convergence raises the prospect of simultaneous pressure on two of the world's most consequential maritime arteries: Iran disrupting traffic through Hormuz while its Houthi allies strengthen their position around Bab al-Mandab.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the shift reflects Tehran's effort to recover leverage as pressure around Hormuz changes.

"Trump's success in pushing back on Iran's maritime threat in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf has made the regime lose the maritime leverage it had, and now it is looking to double down on the Houthis who have proven to be able to impact Red Sea shipping and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the past," Ben Taleblu said.

"As Tehran loses leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, it is trying to wield a knife and a handshake at once: diplomacy with Arab states and a knife in the back via the Houthi offensive," he added.

Iran Calls On Houthis To Prepare To Cut Off Red Sea Gateway — Can The Terror Group Do It?

The latest advance follows the Houthis' capture Thursday of the strategic Red Sea port of Mocha, which was previously held by forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government.

Former U.S. special envoy for Yemen Timothy Lenderking said Friday that the Houthis had spent the years since the 2022 U.N.-brokered truce rebuilding their military strength and are now exploiting the broader Iran conflict to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia.

Speaking during an on-the-record Middle East Institute virtual briefing, Lenderking said the April 2022 truce largely put Yemen's civil war on pause but also "did allow the Houthis to regroup, retrain, refit, restock."

"They're extremely entrepreneurial. They use every opportunity to build their capability, to test their capabilities, such that they are now the most lethal non-state actor in the entire Middle East," Lenderking said.

Lenderking traced the latest round of escalation in part to Iranian Mahan Air flights into Sanaa earlier this summer, which he said brought personnel and equipment intended to support the Houthi war effort, adding that the personnel were from Iran and were "probably IRGC members."

Iran-backed Houthi Threat In Red Sea Could Lead To Major U.s. Policy Shift, Analysts Say

Lenderking said the Houthis are now taking advantage of the wider conflict with Iran to increase their leverage over Riyadh.

"They've seized this opportunity, bringing these various lines of effort together, to put a great deal of pressure on the Yemen government and the Saudis specifically," he said.

On Thursday, a senior Trump administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."

The stakes extend well beyond Yemen.

The Bab al-Mandab is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and serves as the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. About 7% of global oil output passed through the strait in June, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. Disruption can force ships to reroute around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding significant time and cost to voyages.

Expert Warns Of 'General Escalation' Of Fighting If Houthis Resume Red Sea Campaign

Ben Taleblu said the speed of the Houthi advance exposed vulnerabilities in the Saudi-led effort to contain the group.

"The U.S. should help the Saudis stymie the Houthi advance," he said. "The inability of the Saudis to prevent the Houthis from taking the strategic port city of Mocha, for example, does not bode well for what may come."

Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen adviser at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the danger extends beyond the territory captured. Retreating government forces, he said, left behind military equipment that could strengthen the Houthis on other fronts.

"People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere."

The developments mark a dramatic reversal from the relative calm that followed the 2022 truce and leave Washington and its regional allies confronting a growing question: whether the Houthi advance can be contained without opening another direct U.S. military front as American forces remain focused on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Trump Wants Voters to Pretend He’s on the Ballot
description: Chris...
fullText:
But Republican midterm candidates are hoping everyone forgets he exists.

The balance of commentary on the GOP’s midterm pep rally in Dallas has focused on President Donald Trump’s outlandish and unlikely scheme to bribe voters with a $5,000 payoff should the Republicans prevail in the midterms. That’s understandable, since Trump’s scheme is brazenly illegal—as was the case when Elon Musk promised a similarly sleazy $1 million “lottery” windfall to right-leaning voters in Wisconsin’s 2025 balloting for state Supreme Court justices. (The only material difference here is that Musk was in a position to deliver the promised bribe, while Trump very much is not.)

Yet such rank corruption is increasingly the Republican Party’s business model—which is why the mini-convention also featured blaring violations of the Hatch Act, with both Attorney General Todd Blanche and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent electioneering for the GOP in a register only marginally less corrupt than their boss’s spectacle of transactional grift. (In Bessent’s case, the bond markets reacted with an alacrity that our judicial system now conspicuously lacks.) Until we regain a viable system of genuine constitutional oversight, the most urgent question before our flailing political order is whether Trump’s pitch to voters is likely to work. By this, I don’t mean the president’s bribery ploy but the political appeal he also made in Dallas: “Pretend that I’m on the ballot” in November’s midterm elections.

Sure, that’s a predictable come-on from a chief executive who sees all the basic operations of government as an extension of his own ego. At the same time, it’s a likely recipe to kill off any Republican prospects for keeping the party’s present governing trifecta intact. Trump is a stunningly unpopular president, reaching a nadir of approval in the low to mid 30s just last week. That’s why a strong contingent of vulnerable GOP candidates running in swing states were no shows to what Republicans were calling Dallas’s “Trump-a-palooza.” It’s also why a growing number of similarly situated Republican hopefuls have been scrubbing either the person of Trump or key elements of his governing agenda from their campaign websites. Pretending that Trump is on the ballot is pretty much the last thing they want to do.

The strategy behind making the GOP midterms a referendum on Trump is a revival of the one that won him the 2024 election: target “low propensity” voters otherwise tuned out of politics with sops to their short-term self-interest. This is what yielded such pseudopopulist proposals as the cynically sunsetted “no tax on tips” revenue policy and deductions of interest on auto loans; it’s also the clear logic behind the $5,000 bribery scheme (which, like so many other gruesome features of our late-stage oligarchy, was previewed in Idiocracy).

But the glaring problem with continuing to flog the low-propensity strategy is that midterm cycles simply don’t work that way: They run mostly on motivated base voters, who are paying very close attention to politics. (On top of which, of course, midterm balloting almost always favors the party that’s out of power in the Oval Office.)

What’s more, there’s strong evidence that even the low-propensity voters whom the 2024 Trump campaign successfully recruited are experiencing serious buyer’s remorse. Pollster G. Elliott Morris has distilled the findings from eight months’ worth of surveys tracking the positions of voters on the issues most important to them with their support for a major-party presidential candidate in 2024. His key takeaway is very bad news for the promoters of the Dallas convention and the strategy behind it: “voters who are less likely to turn out to vote are actually much less approving of Trump overall and on key issues.” A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released at the end of August found that 15 percent of respondents who voted for Trump in 2024 said that they might or would vote differently if given the choice again; 6 percent said they regretted voting altogether. Only 58 percent of Trump voters in the survey said they were very confident they’d make the right choice in 2024—a marked drop-off from the 74 percent saying as much in April 2025. (The segment of voters sorry that they’d voted at all, meanwhile, was just 1 percent back then.)

These dynamics supply a whole bevy of reasons why the GOP should be urging voters to pay no attention to the bloated, bellicose orange man behind the curtain. Yet after spending the past decade transforming the Republican Party into an authoritarian cult of personality, there’s no other clear path before them. If party strategists were to plow ahead without trying to marshal a new model army of low-propensity voters, things would look considerably worse for them: Morris’s polls show a clear leftward shift in the likely 2026 electorate—together with nearly every midterm survey of the generic Republican and Democratic ballots. Indeed, a recent Gallup poll found that 49 percent of likely 2026 voters identify as Democrats, with just 39 percent aligning with the GOP—the largest such margin since 2008, when Democrats last secured a supermajority in Congress, along with the White House. Half of self-identified independent voters—the swing constituency in many past midterm cycles—now say they lean Democratic.

Even the MAGA movement’s quasi-mythic hold on white working-class voters is eroding. Prior to the 2018 blue-wave midterms, voters in this prime Trump electoral stronghold supported his economic program by margins of 30 percent and more; now, they disapprove of his handling of the economy by a 14-to-30 percent margin. It’s far from clear how Republicans intend to reverse these trends in a two-month span, but one surefire way to make them worse is to continue acting like Donald Trump is on the ballot.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel
Editor and Publisher, The Nation

CAPE TOWN, South Africa (AP) — The Trump administration has provided a $99.6 million loan to a U.S.-owned cell phone network operator in Africa to expand American tech presence on a continent where China's Huawei is a leading player.

The loan from the U.S. government's Export-Import Bank was announced by the operator Africell on Friday. It is the only U.S.-owned cell network operator in Africa.

Africell said in a statement the loan would "boost U.S.-based employment in the telecommunications sector and strengthen American technology leadership abroad." It said the money would allow it to invest specifically in American and European technology for its operations in the southern African country of Angola.

Africell also operates in Congo, Sierra Leone and Gambia, it said.

Huawei is the world's biggest supplier of telecommunications network equipment and is estimated to have supplied more than half the 4G and 5G network infrastructure in Africa.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration raised national security concerns about Huawei in his first term and has moved to counter its global expansion.

The U.S. has lobbied Western allies to avoid using the Chinese company's products in their high-speed wireless networks, while U.S. prosecutors have accused Huawei of stealing technology, plotting to steal U.S. trade secrets and committing wire and bank fraud, among other crimes.

A criminal racketeering trial against Huawei opened in New York this week. Huawei said the U.S. allegations are "demonstrably false."

The Trump administration has also moved to counter China's large influence in other areas in Africa, including in the extraction of critical minerals and rare earth elements that are key in the production of electronics, other new technologies and defense systems.

title: As Trump squeezes the International Criminal Court, more countries are leaving

THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — As the United States ratchets up the pressure on the International Criminal Court, sanctioning two more high-ranking staff members in recent weeks, a small but growing number of the global tribunal's member states have announced they will quit the institution.

The recent departure of Venezuela and Chad brings the number of countries to pull out of the court in the past year to five, joining Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. The surge in withdrawals comes as the ICC faces hostility from Washington and a leadership crisis after ousting its own chief prosecutor.

"Five countries so far have announced plans to withdraw from the Rome Statute, and we welcome more announcements in the future," a spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told The Associated Press.

The Rome Statute established the ICC in 2002 as the court of last resort to prosecute individuals responsible for the world's most heinous atrocities: war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression. Based in The Hague, it takes on cases when nations are unable or unwilling to prosecute crimes on their own territory.

"The ICC regrets any decision to depart from the collective effort to end impunity for the most serious international crimes," the court's spokesperson Oriane Maillet told the AP.

In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the U.S. was launching a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty."

Rubio said he will pressure the court's 125 member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organizations that work with the court and ban staff from traveling to the United States. Trump's administration already has sanctioned a dozen ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court has issued for top Israeli officials over the war in Gaza and investigations into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.

The Central African country of Chad specifically cited the United States in its decision to withdraw. Its Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul said in a statement that in a phone call with a U.S. official on July 23, "the American side expressed its concerns regarding the functioning of this institution and requested that Chad reconsider" its membership.

Four days later, Chad said it would leave the ICC.

Iva Vukušić, a researcher at Utrecht University, told the AP that the U.S. campaign will lay bare just how committed countries are to the court. "Are they willing to defend it if it costs them something real?" she said.

The State Department told AP the U.S. would call upon nations that "enjoy the benefits of the U.S. security umbrella" to reject the ICC.

It's not just pressure from Trump that is sending ICC members toward the exit door.

The ruling military juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger blamed selective justice. The ICC has become an "instrument of neocolonial repression in the hands of imperialism," the trio said when they announced their departures last year.

A coup ousted Niger's democratically elected government in 2023. Since then, a military junta has abandoned longtime partners and has formed new alliances instead, including with Russia, where President Vladimir Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant linked to the war in Ukraine. Mali and Burkina Faso have undergone similar transformations.

"These countries are ruled by authoritarian leaders who want to avoid accountability for the harms they are inflicting on their own people," Mel O'Brien, an associate professor of international law at the University of Western Australia, told the AP.

Burundi similarly accused the court of focusing too much on conflicts in Africa when, in 2017, it became the first country to leave the ICC. The court had opened an investigation into the East African nation earlier that year.

Most of the court's initial investigations were into African countries, though most requested the involvement of the ICC.

South Africa and Gambia also announced in 2017 that they would leave but later changed course.

A change of government can also bring a country back into the fold. Hungary announced it would quit the court in 2025 but following the election of a new government, the country's parliament voted to stay.

The court also had an active investigation in the Philippines when then-President Rodrigo Duterte said his country would leave the ICC. In 2019 the Southeast Asian country became the second country to leave but as withdrawal from the court is not retroactive, the investigation continued.

Duterte is now in ICC detention in the Netherlands awaiting trial on charges of crimes against humanity for deadly anti-drug crackdowns he allegedly oversaw while in office. Opening statements are set for November.

An investigation into possible crimes committed by Venezuelan security forces under former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro will continue despite the country's announcement last month that it will also leave the ICC.

In a statement, the country's Foreign Minister Félix Plasencia said the court had been "instrumentalized to deepen inequalities among peoples and disregard their right to self-determination and sovereignty."

Venezuela is currently in the middle of U.S.-backed talks between the ruling party and the opposition following Maduro's capture in January by U.S. forces.

Ukraine is the court's most recent addition. The country joined in 2025 and previously had signed an agreement to give the court jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, following the outbreak of hostilities with Russia in 2014.

Joining the court was "Ukraine's way of saying that accountability for the gravest crimes cannot be optional, and that we intend to help build that system of justice," the country's ambassador to the Netherlands, Andriy Kostin, told AP.

title: Trump officials scramble to manage fallout after his $5K check pledge to all Americans
description: President Donald Trump blindsided many of his own administration officials and allies with his vow to pay all American adults $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress, prompting an internal scra...
fullText:
President Donald Trump blindsided many of his own administration officials and allies with his vow to pay all American adults $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress, prompting an internal scramble on Thursday to backfill the proposal's specifics, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.

Trump made the pledge during his speech at the GOP's midterm convention after discussing it with only a small circle of close political advisers, including Jason Miller and James Blair, a Trump political adviser told CNN. That left most officials across the administration unprepared to manage the fallout of a $1 trillion proposal that has already faced widespread blowback over its price tag and feasibility.

Several Republican lawmakers immediately panned the idea as a misguided ploy ahead of November's midterm elections that would be nearly impossible to pass through Congress — not to mention one that would violate many of the party's core economic principles. Even on the convention floor, some attendees were skeptical.

"I'm not into free stuff," Arlington small business owner Wilma May told CNN in Dallas. "I would prefer him to give $5,000 towards paying down the deficit."

The vow also alarmed GOP economists and some close Trump allies, some of whom dismissed it as a poor attempt to effectively bribe voters to keep Republicans in power.

"It's a mystery that everybody's trying to get to the bottom of, whose idea this was," said Stephen Moore, an outside economic adviser to Trump, who opposes the idea. "The problem with sending people checks is it actually has a negative economic consequence."

Trump offered few details about the proposal during his speech on Wednesday night, suggesting only that it might draw on revenue collected as a result of tariffs on foreign goods. Trump has previously floated a series of other "dividends" for all Americans funded by tariff revenue or other savings, but has yet to deliver on them.

On Thursday, White House officials spent the morning racing to sort out the logistics required to make good on this latest unprecedented promise, one official said.

But a subsequent fact sheet released by the White House indicated that those efforts remained a work in progress; it provided no details on how the government envisioned funding the payments or where the money would come from.

"The same leadership that shattered the old limits of what Washington thought possible is now prepared to put $5,000 directly into Americans' pockets," the White House said, without providing specifics.

A White House official disputed the notion that Trump had caught his aides off guard, telling CNN that he had "discussed this idea with his senior staff in the lead up to the speech. There was no surprise."

In a statement, White House spokesman Davis Ingle did not directly address the prospect of paying all American adults $5,000 if Republicans keep the House and Senate.

"The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump," he said. "With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results."

Trump's surprise pledge comes as he struggles to combat rising voter frustration over the cost of living and his economic policies. For months, polling has shown Americans deeply dissatisfied with the president's handling of inflation.

The ongoing war with Iran has only worsened the broader economic environment facing Republicans, sending gas and diesel prices soaring once again in recent weeks, with no clear end in sight. As the GOP gathered in Dallas this week, both the global and US benchmark prices for oil rose above the $100-per-barrel mark, and diesel hit a record $5.98 a gallon, on average, on Thursday.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed the affordability concerns, dismissing the term on Wednesday night as an issue ginned up by Democrats to damage him politically and insisting that that US is in the midst of a "the most successful two years financially and every other way."

Yet in a tacit acknowledgment that economic woes are weighing on the GOP, the administration in recent weeks has increasingly sought to highlight steps aimed at lowering some everyday costs, like the price of ground beef and certain medicines.

Trump, who signed off on sending Americans two rounds of $1,200 stimulus checks during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, has repeatedly returned to the idea of sending cash directly to voters as a way to win political support.

Last year, he floated the prospect of $5,000 "DOGE dividends" tied to the supposed savings created by his slashing of the federal workforce. More recently, Trump vowed to send out $2,000 checks funded by tariff revenue. Neither have happened.

Trump's latest proposal faces even longer odds — a reality that prompted many skeptics, including some Trump allies, to dismiss the idea as a purely political maneuver.

"For the record, I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this admin, but am strongly against bread and circus bribes," Joe Lonsdale, a GOP donor close to Donald Trump Jr., wrote Wednesday night on X. Lonsdale co-hosted a major fundraiser on the sidelines of the convention Wednesday night with Trump Jr. and other high-profile Republicans, sources familiar with the event said.

Congressional Republicans would need to write and pass legislation authorizing the more than $1 trillion in payments – a sum that would equal more than half of the amount the government spent on all discretionary spending in the 2025 fiscal year, according to the Congressional Budget Office. And while some lawmakers immediately backed the idea — Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio pledged to have a bill ready by November — the proposal surprised GOP leadership, who had not had any prior discussions about it, a person familiar with the matter said.

In a Fox News interview airing Thursday, Trump seemed to acknowledge that Congress would need to approve the proposal, blaming Democrats for standing in the way of his ability to follow through on the pledge sooner. But he then contradicted himself, saying in a CBS interview that while Republicans "will do it if we needed it," he believed he could deliver the payments without congressional action.

The idea also hinges on the president's party keeping control of the House and Senate — a midterm outcome that would defy polling trends and decades of political precedent.

"The danger he has is that the way it was rolled out, it will sound like a gimmick," said former House GOP Speaker Newt Gingrich, who added that he's previously talked to Trump about distributing money generated by tariffs, but was surprised Wednesday night's announcement.

There are also myriad economic concerns that likely make such a proposal unlikely to become anything more than a political talking point. Trump's proposal would blow a $1.2 trillion hole in the federal budget, which is already contending with a swiftly-rising debt level, according to at least two estimates.

Tariffs wouldn't come close to covering the tab. New tariffs in 2027 would only raise enough revenue to pay for about one-tenth of the cost, according to the Tax Foundation, a right-leaning think tank.

"A deficit-financed dividend payment of this scale would signal to markets that the US is not serious about getting its fiscal house in order," Erica York, a senior economist at the foundation, said in a statement. "It would risk further rises in interest rates, add to inflationary pressures, and worsen the very problems that are trying to be 'solved' by the proposal."

Another federal budget watchdog group called the idea "fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious."

"This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation, and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy," Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement.

Trump's proposal comes as the United States is digging itself into an ever-deeper debt hole. The federal debt hit a record $40 trillion in mid-August, an inauspicious milestone that will have consequences for Americans, businesses and the government for years to come.

Even without the dividend checks, the federal government is forecast to run a budget deficit of nearly $1.9 trillion in fiscal year 2027, which starts October 1.

"It's not an economic growth proposal," said Moore, adding even if Republicans had the money to spend, it'd be better invested elsewhere. "With that amount of money you could cut the payroll tax by one or two percentage points, you could cut income tax by two to three points. That would actually provide an economic incentive."

CNN's Steve Contorno contributed to this report.

title: Trump wants to send Americans money. Congress and economists don't seem thrilled with the idea
description: Donald Trump's pitch to send Americans $5,000 checks should Republicans prevail in the November midterms is drawing scorn from some members of Congress — the very people who have constitutional author...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Donald Trump's pitch to send Americans $5,000 checks should Republicans prevail in the November midterms is drawing scorn from some members of Congress — the very people who have constitutional authority over federal spending.

Economists and other political observers are voicing concerns about the potential effects on inflation and the national balance sheet. Taken together, it's a swift reaction that makes clear that Trump's dubious election-year gambit is likely little more than another grand promise from a politician with a long history of them.

"Donald Trump is a known liar. This is the biggest liar to ever serve in government. Period," said Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat who was in Dallas on Thursday as part of his party's effort to counter Republicans' midterm convention. "The dividend is not happening."

Trump previously pledged to use savings from the Department of Government Efficiency and revenue from tariffs on foreign imports to distribute payments of $2,000 or more, but none of that came to pass.

His latest idea comes as the U.S. economy is reckoning with persistent inflation and rising interest rates, two forces that have politically undermined Republicans after previously helping them reclaim power from Democrats. Trump claimed the payments would be possible because of the economy's strength, yet consumer sentiment is weak as gasoline prices are increasing because of the war with Iran and wages are struggling to keep pace with inflation.

A few of Trump's allies embraced the idea, including Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, who said he would prepare legislation for the payments. But critics accused him of trying to buy votes at a time when Republicans are trying to maintain slim majorities in Congress.

"I don't know about you all, but frankly I'm insulted by the notion that my vote this November could be bought for 5k," Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who is one of Trump's least favorite lawmakers, wrote on social media. "Not to mention the inflation this would cause."

Rep. Ted Lieu, vice chairman of the House Democratic caucus, outright mocked the president.

"If Democrats flip the House and Senate everyone will get a $10,000 dividend, and a pony, and free ice cream for life," he posted on social media. "(Folks can also choose free yogurt for life, because we're Democrats after all)."

The president's proposal, unveiled in his nearly two-hour speech Wednesday night in Dallas, would carry a price tag exceeding $1.3 trillion if Congress were to authorize $5,000 payments to the nation's 270 million adults.

The Treasury already is running a current annual deficit approaching $1.8 trillion, and the total national debt topped $40 trillion this year. According to Treasury Department data, that interest expense for fiscal year 2026 will come to about $1.27 trillion, similar to the projected cost of Trump's idea.

Economists raised concerns about inflationary effects from such a large infusion of cash into the economy.

Michael Strain, director of economic policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right think tank, said Trump would be repeating the same policy mistake as his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden.

As part of his 2021 pandemic relief package, Biden provided $1,400 payments to most Americans, which Strain had warned at the time would spark inflation.

"But Mr. Trump's proposal would be worse than the Biden stimulus in the sense that in 2026 the economy already has an inflation problem," Strain said, while Biden's policy was intended to shore up an economy disrupted by COVID-19.

"Trump would be pouring gasoline on lit inflationary embers and hoping it wouldn't ignite," Strain said.

At the center-left Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, senior policy director Marc Goldwein agreed with the comparison to Biden's policy and emphasized the potential impact on the deficit.

"The idea that we've had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable," he said. "We don't have surpluses to give away."

The financial markets appeared to be unimpressed by Trump's promise. Interest rates on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note climbed above 4.9% in Thursday afternoon trading, meaning that the cost of mortgages and auto loans will likely rise in ways that hurt the middle class.

Many Republicans, including from Trump's inner circle, are in a difficult spot after they've spent years blasting Biden and other Democrats for their spending.

As recently as last week, Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Trump's predecessor when asked about current price levels and consumer concern.

In the White House briefing room, Vance said at once that he was not interested in assigning blame while in the same answer noting "how endemic inflation became during the Biden administration."

Bessent told CNBC that Biden and his allies "torched the American people" with their approach. "Almost 50 percent of the great inflation came from the out-of-control spending that went on then," he argued.

Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, one of Trump's press secretaries during his first presidency, ran into the same conundrum Thursday — after the president's speech — when she shared on social media her appearance on Fox Business Channel.

"You do not build a strong economy by giving things away," Sanders said.

"At the end of the day, though, somebody has to pick up the check," she continued, "and it's the taxpayers that will ultimately pay the price."

Goldwein said ultimately that political and constitutional realities could spare the president.

"You never want to say it's impossible," he said. "But within the confines of the law, at least the law as everybody understands it, the president does not have legal authority to send people $5,000 per adult, and he needs Congress to pass a law."

title: Chip Roy on Trump dividends: ‘Dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms’
description: Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) criticized President Trump’s Wednesday proposal to give every American adult a $5,000 dividend if the GOP wins the midterms, as other Republicans have also voiced skepticism ab...
fullText:
Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) criticized President Trump's Wednesday proposal to give every American adult a $5,000 dividend if the GOP wins the midterms, as other Republicans have also voiced skepticism about the pledge.

"Some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms," Roy wrote Thursday on social platform X, pushing back on venture capitalist Clint Brown's defense of the president's proposal.

On Wednesday, the staunchly conservative Texan estimated that giving every American adult $5,000 would cost the federal government $1.2 trillion in fiscal 2027.

"Dear certain friends… deficits aside - you could almost ZERO out taxes for married parents of dependents up to $200,000 over 10 years!" Roy wrote on X.

Trump made the promise Wednesday, saying he will send the dividends to every adult citizen only if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate in November.

"Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," he said at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas.

There are roughly 270 million adults in the U.S. The president did not offer specifics on the proposal outside of saying recipients could only spend the money in the U.S.

"We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money," Trump remarked. "We don't want you going to China, to Germany."

It is unclear whether Congress would have to pass legislation approving the dividends. When the president proposed sending $2,000 tariff dividend checks to Americans last year, he claimed he didn't "believe" he needed congressional approval to do so. The tariff dividend checks proposal never came to fruition.

Trump made Wednesday's promise less than a month after the U.S. national debt crossed the $40 trillion threshold. The debt has increased by more than $3.8 trillion since the start of the president's second term.

Roy's estimated cost of the dividend is slightly less than the amount the federal government has paid in interest on the debt this fiscal year: $1.27 trillion. The U.S. government has paid more than $1 trillion in interest on the debt in each of the last three fiscal years.

Roy, who is departing Congress after losing the GOP primary runoff for Texas attorney general in May, was not alone among Republicans in opposing Trump's proposal.

Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) called the idea a "socialist vote-buying scheme" early Thursday morning.

"Sadly, most 'conservatives' don't even know (or care) that the president doesn't have the constitutional authority to spend $$, or send out 'dividend' checks without Congress," Good wrote later Thursday on X.

title: Iran strikes U.S. jets after Trump promises war to end after midterms

fullText:
Several U.S. fighter jets at a Jordanian military base were damaged in Iranian strikes on Wednesday, sources tell CBS News. Iran's state media had previously said Tehran targeted U.S. assets across the region in retaliation for American attacks on Iranian oil tankers.Yemen's Houthis seized the key Red Sea port of Mokha on Thursday, according to military sources speaking to the AFP and Reuters.
